claim: 27% of A. cervicornis were disease resistant prior to a thermal anomaly.
source: We determined that 27% of A. cervicornis were disease resistant prior to a thermal anomaly.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from disease exposure trials conducted in August 2015 before bleaching occurred.

claim: Disease resistance was largely lost during a bleaching event.
source: However, disease resistance was largely lost during a bleaching event because of more compromised coral hosts or increased pathogenic dose/virulence.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing disease susceptibility before and after bleaching.

claim: There was no tradeoff between disease resistance and temperature tolerance.
source: There was no tradeoff between disease resistance and temperature tolerance; disease susceptibility was independent of Symbiodinium strain.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that disease-resistant genotypes did not show enhanced temperature tolerance.

claim: Disease susceptibility was independent of Symbiodinium strain.
source: There was no tradeoff between disease resistance and temperature tolerance; disease susceptibility was independent of Symbiodinium strain.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing disease susceptibility across different Symbiodinium strains.

claim: Susceptibility to temperature stress creates an increased risk in disease-associated mortality.
source: The present study shows that susceptibility to temperature stress creates an increased risk in disease-associated mortality, and only rare genets may maintain or gain infectious disease resistance under high temperature.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing increased disease mortality after bleaching.

claim: Only rare genets may maintain or gain infectious disease resistance under high temperature.
source: The present study shows that susceptibility to temperature stress creates an increased risk in disease-associated mortality, and only rare genets may maintain or gain infectious disease resistance under high temperature.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that only one or two genets maintained disease resistance after bleaching.

claim: A. cervicornis populations in the lower Florida Keys harbor few existing genotypes that are resistant to both warming and disease.
source: We conclude that A. cervicornis populations in the lower Florida Keys harbor few existing genotypes that are resistant to both warming and disease.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that most genotypes lost disease resistance after bleaching.

claim: Genetic diversity within a population leads to varying levels of stress tolerance among individuals.
source: Genetic diversity within a population leads to varying levels of stress tolerance among individuals (Sorensen et al., 2001), and is critical for species survival and persistence in a changing climate (Hoffmann and Sgrò, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Genetic diversity is critical for species survival and persistence in a changing climate.
source: Genetic diversity within a population leads to varying levels of stress tolerance among individuals (Sorensen et al., 2001), and is critical for species survival and persistence in a changing climate (Hoffmann and Sgrò, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Certain corals are more resilient to stress than others.
source: It is well known that certain corals are more resilient to stress than others, and the genotype of the coral plays a significant role in determining thermal resistance (Edmunds, 1994; Fitt et al., 2009; Baird et al., 2009; Baums et al., 2013; Kenkel et al., 2013), with a heritable component (Kenkel et al., 2013; Dixon et al., 2015; Polato et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The genotype of the coral plays a significant role in determining thermal resistance.
source: It is well known that certain corals are more resilient to stress than others, and the genotype of the coral plays a significant role in determining thermal resistance (Edmunds, 1994; Fitt et al., 2009; Baird et al., 2009; Baums et al., 2013; Kenkel et al., 2013), with a heritable component (Kenkel et al., 2013; Dixon et al., 2015; Polato et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Thermal resistance has a heritable component.
source: It is well known that certain corals are more resilient to stress than others, and the genotype of the coral plays a significant role in determining thermal resistance (Edmunds, 1994; Fitt et al., 2009; Baird et al., 2009; Baums et al., 2013; Kenkel et al., 2013), with a heritable component (Kenkel et al., 2013; Dixon et al., 2015; Polato et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Tolerance to stress may be a result of different symbiotic algal species (Symbiodinium spp.).
source: Tolerance to stress may also be a result of different symbiotic algal species (Symbiodinium spp.) or even of different genotypes (i.e. strains) of certain Symbiodinium species that reside within the coral host (Grégoire et al., 2017; Parkinson and Baums, 2014; Fabricius et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Tolerance to stress may be a result of different genotypes (i.e. strains) of certain Symbiodinium species.
source: Tolerance to stress may also be a result of different symbiotic algal species (Symbiodinium spp.) or even of different genotypes (i.e. strains) of certain Symbiodinium species that reside within the coral host (Grégoire et al., 2017; Parkinson and Baums, 2014; Fabricius et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Infectious disease outbreaks and ocean acidification are affecting coral populations in combination with temperature anomalies.
source: Furthermore, additional threats to corals, such as infectious disease outbreaks and ocean acidification, are affecting populations in combination with temperature anomalies (Hoegh-Guldberg et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Many species possess the ability to produce broad-spectrum defense mechanisms.
source: Evidence suggests that many species possess the ability to produce broad-spectrum defense mechanisms (de Nadal et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Coral populations showing resilience to high water temperatures constitutively frontload the expression of genes related to heat tolerance in concert with several genes influencing the host innate immune response.
source: Similarly, coral populations showing resilience to high water temperatures constitutively frontload the expression of genes related to heat tolerance in concert with several genes influencing the host innate immune response (Barshis et al., 2013), suggesting these corals may also have evolved the general ability to tolerate a multitude of threats.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Corals that frontload heat tolerance genes may have evolved the general ability to tolerate a multitude of threats.
source: Similarly, coral populations showing resilience to high water temperatures constitutively frontload the expression of genes related to heat tolerance in concert with several genes influencing the host innate immune response (Barshis et al., 2013), suggesting these corals may also have evolved the general ability to tolerate a multitude of threats.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from cited research.

claim: Acropora cervicornis was one of the most common corals within the shallow reefs of the Western Atlantic and Caribbean several decades ago.
source: The Caribbean coral species, Acropora cervicornis, was one of the most common corals within the shallow reefs of the Western Atlantic and Caribbean several decades ago (Pandolfi, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Over the last 40 years multiple stressors including infectious disease, high sea surface temperatures, overfishing and habitat degradation have caused a 95% population reduction in A. cervicornis.
source: However, over the last 40 years multiple stressors including infectious disease, high sea surface temperatures, overfishing and habitat degradation have caused a 95% population reduction (Acropora Biological Review Team, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: A. cervicornis is listed as threatened under the U.S. Endangered Species Act.
source: A. cervicornis is now listed as threatened under the U.S. Endangered Species Act.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of regulatory status.

claim: Significant loss of Caribbean Acropora species was attributed to white-band disease outbreaks that spread throughout the region in the late 1970's and early 1980's.
source: Significant loss of Caribbean Acropora species was attributed to white-band disease outbreaks that spread throughout the region in the late 1970' s and early 1980' s (Aronson and Precht, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The pathogen causing white band disease is likely bacterial in nature.
source: While the disease-causing agent of white band has not been identified, the pathogen is likely bacterial in nature (Peters, 1984; Kline and Vollmer, 2011; Sweet et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: White band disease continues to cause mortality across populations.
source: This disease continues to cause mortality across populations (Miller et al., 2014) and especially Florida (Precht et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: 6% of the A. cervicornis tested in Panama were resistant to white-band disease.
source: For example, 6% of the A. cervicornis tested in Panama were resistant to white-band disease (Vollmer and Kline, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Long term monitoring of A. palmata in the US Virgin Islands indicated that 6% of 48 known genets showed no disease signs over eight years.
source: Additionally, long term monitoring of A. palmata in the US Virgin Islands indicated that 6% of 48 known genets showed no disease signs over eight years; perhaps indicating a small disease resistant population (Rogers and Muller, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: There are disease resistant variants within some locations, although they may be low in abundance.
source: Hence, there are disease resistant variants within some locations, although they may be low in abundance.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from cited research on disease resistance in Panama and USVI.

claim: Anomalously high water temperatures are increasing the probability of disease occurrence throughout the Caribbean.
source: Regardless, anomalously high water temperatures are increasing the probability of disease occurrence throughout the Caribbean (Muller et al., 2008; Miller et al., 2009; Randall and van Woesik, 2015) and field monitoring suggests that bleached corals are more susceptible to disease (Muller et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Field monitoring suggests that bleached corals are more susceptible to disease.
source: Regardless, anomalously high water temperatures are increasing the probability of disease occurrence throughout the Caribbean (Muller et al., 2008; Miller et al., 2009; Randall and van Woesik, 2015) and field monitoring suggests that bleached corals are more susceptible to disease (Muller et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Recent field-based observations suggest that there is a negative association between heat tolerance and disease susceptibility in A. cervicornis.
source: Alternatively, recent field-based observations suggest that there is a negative association between heat tolerance and disease susceptibility in A. cervicornis (Merselis et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Tropical reef-building corals gain a majority of their carbon from their algal symbionts.
source: Tropical reef-building corals gain a majority of their carbon from their algal symbionts (Muscatine et al., 1984) and thus the stress response of the coral animal has to be viewed in the context of its symbiotic partner or partners.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Prolonged temperature stress causes the disassociation between the coral host and the single-celled algae (Symbiodinium spp) residing within its tissues, a phenomenon called bleaching.
source: Prolonged temperature stress causes the disassociation between the coral host and the single-celled algae (Symbiodinium spp) residing within its tissues, a phenomenon called bleaching.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about coral bleaching.

claim: Studies of the immune protein concentrations within corals indicate a suppressed immune system when corals bleached.
source: Studies of the immune protein concentrations within corals indicate a suppressed immune system when corals bleached (Mydlarz et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Immune-related host gene activity is suppressed for at least a year after bleaching occurs, at least for some species.
source: Furthermore, immune-related host gene activity is suppressed for at least a year after bleaching occurs, at least for some species (Pinzón et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Some coral species harbor multiple Symbiodinium species in the same colony or over environmental gradients, while others associate with only one Symbiodinium species.
source: While some coral species harbor multiple Symbiodinium species in the same colony or over environmental gradients, others associate with only one Symbiodinium species (LaJeunesse, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Symbiodinium species differ in their heat tolerance.
source: Symbiodinium species differ in their heat tolerance (Berkelmans and van Oppen, 2006), however, evidence of an association between Symbiodinium species identity and coral host disease susceptibility, is not well studied and equivocal (Correa et al., 2009; Rouzé et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Evidence of an association between Symbiodinium species identity and coral host disease susceptibility is not well studied and equivocal.
source: Symbiodinium species differ in their heat tolerance (Berkelmans and van Oppen, 2006), however, evidence of an association between Symbiodinium species identity and coral host disease susceptibility, is not well studied and equivocal (Correa et al., 2009; Rouzé et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Acropora cervicornis can harbor several species of Symbiodinium.
source: Acropora cervicornis can harbor several species of Symbiodinium (Baums et al., 2010), but it is often dominated by Symbiodinium 'fitti' (nominem nudum).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: A. cervicornis is often dominated by Symbiodinium 'fitti'.
source: Acropora cervicornis can harbor several species of Symbiodinium (Baums et al., 2010), but it is often dominated by Symbiodinium 'fitti' (nominem nudum).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Different strains of a single Symbiodinium species can affect coral physiology.
source: Yet, different strains of a single Symbiodinium species can affect coral physiology (Howells et al., 2011) and thus we aimed to determine the influence of Symbiodinium strain diversity on coral disease susceptibility and bleaching in A. cervicornis.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Coral nurseries provide a unique opportunity to test the effect of multiple stressors on coral survival and adaptation in a common garden environment.
source: Coral nurseries provide a unique opportunity to test the effect of multiple stressors on coral survival and adaptation in a common garden environment.
evidence: This claim is based on inference about the utility of coral nurseries for research.

claim: Nurseries propagate colonies via asexual fragmentation providing experimental replicates for each host genotype/S. 'fitti' combination.
source: Nurseries propagate colonies via asexual fragmentation providing experimental replicates for each host genotype/S. 'fitti' combination.
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of nursery practices.

claim: Host genotypes display differences in growth, linear extension, and thermal tolerance, which are maintained within the common garden environment.
source: Host genotypes display differences in growth, linear extension, and thermal tolerance, which are maintained within the common garden environment (Lohr and Patterson, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The photochemical yield (Fv/Fm) of all fragments, prior to visual bleaching in August 2015, averaged 0.457 (± .015 SE).
source: The photochemical yield (Fv/Fm) of all fragments, prior to visual bleaching in August 2015, averaged 0.457 (± .015 SE).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements.

claim: By September 2015, colonies in the nursery had visually bleached after experiencing temperatures ~2°C above historical averages.
source: However, by September 2015, colonies in the nursery had visually bleached after experiencing temperatures ~2°C above historical averages (Figure 1), represented by 8 degree heating weeks under NOAA's Coral Reef Watch products.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and temperature data.

claim: By September 2015, all of the corals had visibly turned white and the photochemical yield of the corals dropped to 0.148 (± 0.008 SE).
source: By this time, all of the corals had visibly turned white and the photochemical yield of the corals dropped to 0.148 (± 0.008 SE).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements.

claim: Fragments in the first three pre-bleaching trials were significantly higher in photochemical yield than the post-bleaching trial.
source: While there was a gradual reduction in photochemical yield from August to September, fragments in the first three pre-bleaching trials were significantly higher than the post-bleaching trial (Figure 2A, Supplementary file 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 1), as expected.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements and statistical analysis.

claim: In the August pre-bleaching trials, there were significant differences among the photochemical efficiency of S. fitti associated with different host genets.
source: In the August pre-bleaching trials, there were significant differences among the photochemical efficiency of S. fitti associated with different host genets (X2 = 51.173, df = 14, p<0.001, Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements and statistical analysis.

claim: Photochemical efficiency differed among S. fitti associated with different host genets after bleaching.
source: Photochemical efficiency also differed among S. fitti associated with different host genets after bleaching (X2 = 24.42, df = 14, p=0.04), although the relative pattern among S. fitti associated with different host genets changed (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements and statistical analysis.

claim: The relative pattern among S. fitti associated with different host genets changed after bleaching.
source: Photochemical efficiency also differed among S. fitti associated with different host genets after bleaching (X2 = 24.42, df = 14, p=0.04), although the relative pattern among S. fitti associated with different host genets changed (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements and statistical analysis.

claim: A total of 25 out of the 75 fragments exposed to the disease homogenate showed signs of white-band-disease-associated mortality within the first seven days after exposure during the August, pre-bleaching trials.
source: A total of 25 out of the 75 fragments exposed to the disease homogenate showed signs of white-band-disease-associated mortality within the first seven days after exposure during the August, pre-bleaching trials.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations.

claim: Only one fragment (genet 46), out of the 75 total fragments showed signs of disease in the control treatment, within the experimental period.
source: Only one fragment (genet 46), out of the 75 total fragments showed signs of disease in the control treatment, within the experimental period.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations.

claim: There was high variation in disease susceptibility among genets, with susceptibility values ranging from 0% to 80%.
source: There was high variation in disease susceptibility among genets, with susceptibility values ranging from 0% to 80% (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations.

claim: Four genets showed complete resistance to the disease homogenate, with no replicate fragments showing any signs of tissue loss after disease exposure.
source: Four genets showed complete resistance to the disease homogenate, with no replicate fragments showing any signs of tissue loss after disease exposure.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations.

claim: The median susceptibility value among the different genets was 20%.
source: The median susceptibility value among the different genets was 20%.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations.

claim: A total of 55 out of 75 fragments lost tissue after exposure to the disease homogenate when bleached.
source: Results differed when the same genets were exposed to the disease homogenate after they were bleached. A total of 55 out of 75 fragments lost tissue after exposure to the disease homogenate.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations.

claim: 13 out of the 75 control fragments died when bleached.
source: Additionally, 13 out of the 75 control fragments died when bleached.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations.

claim: Values ranged from 100% susceptibility to disease-induced mortality within five genets, to one genet that maintained disease tolerance, even when bleached (genet 3).
source: Values ranged from 100% susceptibility to disease-induced mortality within five genets, to one genet that maintained disease tolerance, even when bleached (genet 3; Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations.

claim: Median susceptibility was 80% among the genets when the corals were bleached.
source: Median susceptibility was 80% among the genets when the corals were bleached.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations.

claim: There was no significant effect of the photochemical yield on disease susceptibility during either the pre-bleaching or post-bleaching experiments.
source: The generalized linear model, which tested whether maximum quantum yield affected disease presence or absence for each replicate genotype indicated there was no significant effect of the photochemical yield on disease susceptibility, even within corals exposed to the disease homogenate, during either the pre-bleaching (z = 0.132, p=0.895) or post-bleaching experiments (z = −1.579, p=0.114).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: There was no effect of the average change in photochemical yield within each genotype on disease susceptibility.
source: Also, there was no effect of the average change in photochemical yield within each genotype on disease susceptibility (pre-bleaching: z = 0.555, p=0.579; post-bleaching: z = −0.023, p=0.982).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The treatment effect was significant within both the pre-bleaching and post bleaching trials, with higher disease presence within corals exposed to the disease homogenate.
source: The mixed-effect generalized linear model showed that the treatment effect was significant within both the pre-bleaching (z = 2.263, p=0.0234) and post bleaching trials (z = 3.515, p<0.001), with higher disease presence within corals exposed to the disease homogenate.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: There were no significant differences detected among genotypes within trials.
source: However, there were no significant differences detected among genotypes within trials (pre-bleaching: z = 0.416, p=0.677; post-bleaching: z = −0.243, p=0.808), nor was there a significant interaction between treatment and genotype within each trial (pre-bleaching: z = 0.090, p=0.928; post-bleaching: z = 0.697, p=0.486).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: There was no significant interaction between treatment and genotype within each trial.
source: However, there were no significant differences detected among genotypes within trials (pre-bleaching: z = 0.416, p=0.677; post-bleaching: z = −0.243, p=0.808), nor was there a significant interaction between treatment and genotype within each trial (pre-bleaching: z = 0.090, p=0.928; post-bleaching: z = 0.697, p=0.486).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: There was no difference in disease presence or absence among the three trials that created the pre-bleaching experiment.
source: There was also no difference in disease presence or absence among the three trials that created the pre-bleaching experiment (z = −1.308, p=0.191), suggesting that pooling data from these three trials was appropriate.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: A total of six different S. fitti strains were found within the 15 coral host genets.
source: A total of six different S. fitti strains were found within the 15 coral host genets (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic analysis of experimental samples.

claim: No other Symbiodinium clades have been detected in the Mote in situ nursery A. cervicornis fragments above background levels.
source: Note that no other Symbiodinium clades have been detected in the Mote in situ nursery A. cervicornis fragments above background levels (Parkinson et al., 2018a) or in other offshore A. cervicornis colonies in the Keys (Baums et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: A majority of the host genets tested (11/15) harbored a single S fitti strain consistently through time (strain F421).
source: A majority of the host genets tested (11/15) harbored a single S fitti strain consistently through time (strain F421; Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic analysis of experimental samples.

claim: The other four Symbiodinium strains were associated with a single coral genet each.
source: The other four Symbiodinium strains were associated with a single coral genet each (See Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic analysis of experimental samples.

claim: There was no significant difference in photochemical efficiency between corals harboring the common F421 Symbiodinium strain and those that harbored the other unique strains, pre- and post-bleaching.
source: There was no significant difference in photochemical efficiency between corals harboring the common F421 Symbiodinium strain and those that harbored the other unique strains, pre- and post-bleaching (pre-bleaching yield: t = −0.13, df = 13, p=0.99; post-bleaching yield: t = −0.244, df = 13, p=0.811).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: There was no influence of Symbiodinium strain on the amount of change in photochemical efficiency between the pre- and post-bleaching experiments.
source: Similarly, there was no influence of Symbiodinium strain on the amount of change in photochemical efficiency between the pre- and post-bleaching experiments (change in yield: t = 0.172, df = 13, p=0.866).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: There was no significant difference in disease susceptibility when corals contained the single Symbiodinium strain F421 compared with the other corals that hosted different Symbiodinium strains.
source: There was no significant difference in disease susceptibility when corals contained the single Symbiodinium strain F421 compared with the other corals that hosted different Symbiodinium strains (pre-bleaching disease: X2 = 0.039, df = 1, p=0.842, post-bleaching disease: X2 = 0.079, df = 1, p=0.779; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Among the eleven coral genets that harbored S. 'fitti' F421, disease susceptibility ranged from 0% (genet 3) to 70% (genet 46) during pre-bleaching trials.
source: Among the eleven coral genets that harbored S. 'fitti' F421, disease susceptibility ranged from 0% (genet 3) to 70% (genet 46) during pre-bleaching trials (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations.

claim: S. fitti strain identity did not influence disease susceptibility for the post bleaching exposures.
source: S. fitti strain identity also did not influence disease susceptibility for the post bleaching exposures (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations.

claim: Under pre-bleaching conditions, the tested A. cervicornis genets were almost three times as likely to experience disease-induced mortality when exposed to the disease homogenate over healthy homogenates.
source: Under pre-bleaching conditions, the tested A. cervicornis genets were almost three times as likely to experience disease-induced mortality when exposed to the disease homogenate over healthy homogenates (median Bayesian relative risk = 2.77, Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by Bayesian relative risk analysis of experimental data.

claim: Genets 1, 3, 41 and 44 showed no increase in disease-induced mortality after disease exposure, with median relative risk values near 1.
source: For example, genets 1, 3, 41 and 44 showed no increase in disease-induced mortality after disease exposure, with median relative risk values of these four genets near 1, that is they were resistant.
evidence: This claim is supported by Bayesian relative risk analysis of experimental data.

claim: The 11 other genets showed an increase in disease risk after exposure to the disease homogenate, with statistically significant increased relative risk values for genets 9 and 10.
source: The 11 other genets, however, showed an increase in disease risk after exposure to the disease homogenate (i.e. they were susceptible), with statistically significant increased relative risk values for genets 9 and 10 (Figure 3A, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by Bayesian relative risk analysis of experimental data.

claim: Post-bleaching, the overall likelihood of disease-induced mortality increased by about three-fold when the corals were bleached and exposed to the disease homogenate, compared with corals that were bleached and exposed to the healthy homogenate.
source: Post-bleaching, the overall likelihood of disease-induced mortality increased by about three-fold (median Bayesian relative risk = 3.33, Figure 3B) when the corals were bleached and exposed to the disease homogenate, compared with corals that were bleached and exposed to the healthy homogenate.
evidence: This claim is supported by Bayesian relative risk analysis of experimental data.

claim: Six genets showed a significant increase in disease risk post-bleaching (genets 5, 41, 44, 46, 47, and 50).
source: Again, substantial variation among genets was detected, although there were now six genets that showed a significant increase in disease risk (genets 5, 41, 44, 46, 47, and 50; Figure 3B, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by Bayesian relative risk analysis of experimental data.

claim: Only one genet, genet 7, was affected by disease pre-bleaching, but not post-bleaching.
source: Only one genet, genet 7, was affected by disease pre-bleaching, but not post-bleaching, whereas genet 3 showed apparent complete immunity whether exposed to a disease homogenate when bleached or not.
evidence: This claim is supported by Bayesian relative risk analysis of experimental data.

claim: Genet 3 showed apparent complete immunity whether exposed to a disease homogenate when bleached or not.
source: Only one genet, genet 7, was affected by disease pre-bleaching, but not post-bleaching, whereas genet 3 showed apparent complete immunity whether exposed to a disease homogenate when bleached or not.
evidence: This claim is supported by Bayesian relative risk analysis of experimental data.

claim: There were no differences detected in the bacterial community of the homogenates among trials.
source: There were no differences detected in the bacterial community of the homogenates among trials (F(1,7)=1.42, p = 0.219), nor did a single operational taxonomic unit significantly differ in relative abundance among trials (1,253 OTUs tested using nonparametric Kruskal Wallis tests).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of bacterial community data.

claim: No single operational taxonomic unit significantly differed in relative abundance among trials.
source: There were no differences detected in the bacterial community of the homogenates among trials (F(1,7)=1.42, p = 0.219), nor did a single operational taxonomic unit significantly differ in relative abundance among trials (1,253 OTUs tested using nonparametric Kruskal Wallis tests).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of bacterial community data.

claim: The PERMANOVA analysis showed no statistical difference between the bacterial OTU community of the healthy homogenate and the disease homogenate.
source: The PERMANOVA analysis also showed no statistical difference between the bacterial OTU community of the healthy homogenate and the disease homogenate (F(1,6) = 1.962, p = 0.134), which was primarily because one healthy homogenate sample was similar to the disease homogenate samples (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of bacterial community data.

claim: One healthy homogenate sample was similar to the disease homogenate samples.
source: The PERMANOVA analysis also showed no statistical difference between the bacterial OTU community of the healthy homogenate and the disease homogenate (F(1,6) = 1.962, p = 0.134), which was primarily because one healthy homogenate sample was similar to the disease homogenate samples (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of bacterial community data.

claim: When the one outlier sample was removed there was a significantly higher abundance of Actinobacteria within the healthy samples compared with the diseased samples.
source: However, when the one outlier sample was removed there was a significantly higher abundance of Actinobacteria (X2 = 4.5, df = 1, p = 0.034) and significantly lower abundance of Alphaproteobacteria (X2 = 4.5, df = 1, p = 0.034) within the healthy samples compared with the diseased samples (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of bacterial community data.

claim: When the one outlier sample was removed there was a significantly lower abundance of Alphaproteobacteria within the healthy samples compared with the diseased samples.
source: However, when the one outlier sample was removed there was a significantly higher abundance of Actinobacteria (X2 = 4.5, df = 1, p = 0.034) and significantly lower abundance of Alphaproteobacteria (X2 = 4.5, df = 1, p = 0.034) within the healthy samples compared with the diseased samples (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
